items.name: 10-Minute Planner (study planner)
items.tagline: The planner behind every Korean study vlog.
items.why: Korea's study-planner culture in one book — plan the day in 10-minute blocks, colour them in as you go
story: Open any Korean 'study with me' video and the same planner is on the desk: Motemote's Ten Minute Planner. Each day is a grid of 10-minute blocks; you write your tasks, then colour the blocks as you finish them, so a productive day literally fills with colour.

It started as a tool for exam students and spread to office workers, language learners and anyone who likes seeing their time. There is nothing like it on US shelves — American planners are weekly or hourly; this one is about the ten minutes you actually have.

items.name: Plus Pen 3000 — 36-colour set
items.why: The 0.4 mm water-based pen in every Korean office and classroom for 50 years — rainbow sets aren't sold in the US
story: If the 153 is Korea's ballpoint, the Plus Pen 3000 is its felt-tip. Launched in 1976, the slim black-capped pen with the fine 0.4 mm tip has been used for signing documents, marking up textbooks and drawing in planners ever since — over four billion sold.

The colour sets are where it gets fun: 12, 24, 36 and 60-colour boxes with a tidy row of pastel and vivid caps, loved for colour-coding notes and simple line drawings. It is a Korea-only product; US fineliner sets are a different pen entirely.

highlights.title: 0.4 mm fine tip
highlights.text: Crisp lines for notes, lettering and planner doodles.

highlights.text: Quick-drying, low odour, safe for kids.

items.tagline: Korea's most-loved character, on your desk.
items.why: Ryan's chubby cat Choonsik is the #1 character in Korea; official goods are sold only in Kakao Friends stores
story: Choonsik is the sweet-potato-loving stray cat adopted by Ryan, the lion of Kakao Friends — the characters built into KakaoTalk, the messenger every Korean uses. Since 2020 Choonsik has outsold every other character in the line-up.

Official goods — pen holders, memo pads, mouse pads, keyrings, mini plush — are sold through Kakao Friends stores and the KakaoTalk gift shop, which don't ship abroad. That makes them one of the most requested 'can you bring me…' items from Korea.

items.name: Seoul subway-map poster & postcards
items.tagline: Seoul, drawn by the studio that redesigned its map.
items.why: The Seoul design studio famous for its city maps — posters, postcards and notebooks you can only buy in Korea
story: Zero Per Zero is a small Seoul graphic studio that became famous for redrawing city subway maps as art — Seoul as a heart, Tokyo, New York, Paris. Their Seoul map is the souvenir Koreans themselves buy for friends abroad.
Posters, postcard sets, notebooks and tape in their crisp geometric style are sold through their own shop and museum stores in Seoul. They are not stocked in the US.

items.name: Hand-carved Hangul name seal (도장)
items.why: A personalised wooden seal with your name in Hangul plus red ink — carved to order in Korea, impossible to buy in the US
story: In Korea a seal (dojang) still signs contracts and bank forms, and a carved personal seal is a classic coming-of-age or graduation gift. Seal shops in Insadong carve names in Hangul in minutes, in round or square styles, on boxwood, horn or stone.
We have your name transliterated into Hangul, carved, and shipped with a red ink pad — a small object that is unmistakably Korean and entirely yours. Use it on letters, books, art and planners.

items.name: Najeon mother-of-pearl DIY kit (자개)
items.tagline: Korea's shimmering lacquer craft, at home.
items.why: Najeon — iridescent shell inlay on black lacquer — is Korea's hottest craft-class trend, now in take-home kits
story: Najeon chilgi — mother-of-pearl inlaid in black lacquer — decorated Korean wardrobes and jewellery boxes for a thousand years. In the last few years it has become the most-booked craft class in Seoul, as young Koreans rediscover it on trays, mirrors and phone grips.

The kit gives you a pre-lacquered base, cut shell pieces, tweezers and glue, and a pattern to follow — a crane, peonies, a tiger. Two quiet hours later you have a piece that catches the light like nothing sold in a US craft store.

items.name: Korean knot (매듭) keyring & norigae kit
items.tagline: Tie the knots that hang from hanbok.
items.why: Maedeup — the decorative silk knots of Korean dress — as a bag charm or keyring you tie yourself; nothing like it in US craft aisles
story: Maedeup is the Korean art of decorative knotting — the silk-cord knots and tassels that hang from a hanbok as a norigae. Each knot has a name (dragonfly, chrysanthemum, lotus) and a symmetry that looks impossible until your hands learn it.

This beginner kit has the cords, a tassel, a bead and step-by-step diagrams to tie a traditional knot into a keyring or bag charm. It is the kind of small, beautiful, very Korean object that US craft stores simply don't carry.

items.name: Hanji paper lamp kit (한지 무드등)
items.tagline: Soft light through Korean mulberry paper.
items.why: Hanji, Korea's thousand-year mulberry paper, glows like nothing else — build a small bedside lamp from a kit
story: Hanji is paper made from mulberry bark, strong enough to last centuries and translucent enough to glow. Korean houses once used it on every window and door, which is why Korean interior light is remembered as warm and soft.
This kit builds a small lamp: a wooden frame, sheets of natural and dyed hanji, glue and an LED bulb. Paper the frame, let it dry, and you have a bedside light with a glow US lamp stores can't match.

items.name: Minhwa folk-painting kit (민화)
items.tagline: Tigers, magpies and peonies — Korean folk art you paint.
items.why: Korean folk painting with its grinning tigers and lucky peonies, as an outlined paint-at-home kit — a uniquely Korean colouring project
story: Minhwa are the folk paintings of old Korea — a tiger grinning under a pine tree while a magpie scolds it, peonies for wealth, carp for success. Bold, funny and bright, they were painted by anonymous artists and hung in ordinary homes for luck.

The kit has pre-outlined designs on Korean paper, mineral-style paints and brushes, so you colour like a folk painter. Finished, it frames beautifully and is a conversation piece no US craft store can offer.

items.name: Jogakbo patchwork pouch kit (조각보)
items.tagline: Korean patchwork that looks like stained glass.
items.why: Jogakbo — Korea's translucent ramie patchwork — in a hand-sew pouch kit; a textile craft the US simply doesn't have
story: Jogakbo is the Korean art of sewing leftover scraps of ramie and silk into wrapping cloths, with seams so fine and fabric so sheer that a finished piece hung in a window looks like stained glass. Once a thrifty household craft, it is now shown in museums.

This kit holds pre-cut squares of translucent fabric in soft colours, thread, a needle and a pattern for a small pouch or a window cloth. Slow, meditative hand-sewing, with a result that is unmistakably Korean.

items.name: Korean spoon & chopsticks set (수저)
items.tagline: The flat Korean spoon and chopsticks the US doesn't sell.
items.why: Long flat spoon + slim flat metal chopsticks, the pair on every Korean table; the shape isn't sold in US stores
story: Korea is the only country that eats with a long-handled spoon and flat metal chopsticks together — the sujeo. The spoon is for rice and soup, the chopsticks for side dishes, and the flat shape is a surprise to anyone used to round wooden ones.

Sets in stainless steel or traditional brass (yugi) come boxed and are the standard housewarming and wedding gift. If you cook Korean food in the US, this is the piece of the table you can't buy locally.

items.name: Bojagi wrapping cloths (보자기)
items.tagline: Wrap gifts the Korean way — no paper, no waste.
items.why: Korea's traditional square wrapping cloth, now in modern patterns; wraps gifts and lunch boxes and gets reused for years
story: Bojagi is the square cloth Koreans have wrapped everything in for centuries — gifts, lunch, bedding, a baby. Folded and knotted, it becomes a bag; untied, it is a cloth you keep. Wedding gifts still arrive in bojagi today.

Modern bojagi come in silky polyester or cotton with traditional patterns and fresh colours, in sizes from a jewellery box to a wine bottle. They are reusable, beautiful, and simply not sold in US stores.

items.name: Illustrated griptok phone grips
items.tagline: Korea's phone-grip culture, one illustrator at a time.
items.why: Griptok is a Korean obsession — collapsible phone grips with indie-illustrator art, swapped like stickers; the US only has plain PopSockets
story: In Korea the phone grip is called a griptok and it is a fashion item: every illustrator, character brand and K-pop fandom releases its own, and people own a handful and swap them with the season. The US has PopSockets; Korea has an entire griptok culture.

We pick griptoks from Korean indie illustrators — hand-drawn characters, foods, flowers — in smart-tok or 3M-adhesive styles. They fold flat, prop your phone up, and make it instantly recognisable as yours.

items.name: Quokka character plush & goods
items.why: Dinotaeng's smiling quokka is the indie character Koreans adore; goods sell only through Korean stores and pop-ups
story: Dinotaeng is a small Korean studio whose quokka character — round cheeks, half-closed eyes, permanently content — went from Instagram comics to a cult following. Its message is simple: it's fine to rest, it's fine to be slow.

Plush, keyrings, stickers, mugs and diaries are sold through the studio's Korean store and pop-ups that draw hours-long queues. Not sold in the US, and one of the most asked-for Korean character goods.
